Elizabeth Fritzl -- now 42 -- spent more than two decades in the windowless basement after being drugged, handcuffed and locked up by her father, Josef Fritzl, as an 18-year-old. Kepplinger said the two sets of children were tentatively getting to know one another, adding that the two boys who had lived underground had an unusual way of communicating with each other. "The two boys appeared overawed by the daylight they had never experienced before," said Chief Inspector Leopold Etz. "The real world was completely alien to them... In an interview with the Austrian newspaper, Oesterreich, psychiatrist Max Friedrich, who treated the abducted teenager Natascha Kampusch, estimated it would take "between five and eight years" for the children to recover from their experiences. Another psychologist, Bernd Prosser, told Austrian television that it would be impossible for the four held prisoner underground to lead normal lives. "I am afraid it is too late for that." Kampusch, the Austrian girl abducted as a 10-year-old and held captive in a basement for more than eight years until she escaped in 2007, also offered her help to the family on Tuesday, but questioned the decision to move them from the cellar into psychiatric care. "Pulling them abruptly out of this situation, without transition, to hold them and isolating them to some extent, it can't be good for them," said Kampusch, now 20, in an interview with Austrian TV station Puls 4. "I believe it might have been even better to leave them where they were, but that was probably impossible. This case is not like mine, where that was not my environment. **Learning to live in the light: Inside the recovery of Austria’s cellar family**

*   By Frederik Pleitgen and Laura Smith-Spark, CNN
*   Updated 4:12 p.m. EDT, October 29, 2008

**(CNN)** — Six months after emerging from a windowless subterranean nightmare that shocked the world, Elisabeth Fritzl and her children are making "astonishing" physical and psychological progress, doctors in Austria say, as they take their first cautious steps toward a normal life.

Elisabeth, 42, and five of her six surviving children have spent the last half-year in a specially adapted, highly secured wing of the Mauer psychiatric clinic near Amstetten. There, behind blacked-out windows and strict security perimeters designed to keep intrusive paparazzi at bay, a team of doctors, therapists, and educators has been guiding the family through an unprecedented rehabilitation process.

For 24 years, Elisabeth was held captive in a cramped, soundproof basement built beneath her family’s home by her father, Josef Fritzl. During her quarter-century in the dark, she gave birth to seven children. Three remained in the cellar with her, three were raised upstairs by Josef and his wife, Rosemarie, as "foundlings," and one died shortly after birth. 

Now, the two halves of the shattered family are learning how to become one.

### Relearning the World

The transition from a dark, low-ceilinged bunker to the open world has been a complex medical challenge. 

According to officials at the clinic, the "downstairs" children—Kerstin, 19, Stefan, 18, and Felix, 5—suffered from severe vitamin D deficiency, anemia, and posture problems caused by the cellar's ceiling, which was under six feet high in some areas. Their eyes were painfully sensitive to natural light, requiring them to wear special tinted glasses for months.

Perhaps the biggest milestone in the family's recovery came in June, when Kerstin, the eldest daughter, was brought out of a medically induced coma. It was Kerstin's life-threatening illness in April—and Elisabeth’s desperate pleas to get her to a hospital—that ultimately led to the discovery of the dungeon and the family's rescue. 

Doctors confirm Kerstin has made a remarkable recovery, reuniting with her mother and siblings at the clinic. 

"The physical healing has been faster than expected," Dr. Berthold Kepplinger, director of the Mauer clinic, said in a recent briefing. "The immune systems of the children who lived in the cellar were frail, but with proper nutrition, daylight therapy, and exercise, they have physically stabilized."

For the children who lived underground, basic everyday experiences have been source of wonder. Therapists report that 5-year-old Felix was fascinated by the concept of rain, while 18-year-old Stefan spent hours during his first weeks outdoors simply feeling grass beneath his feet and watching the sky.

### Uniting a Divided Family

Psychologically, the challenge has been monumental. The medical team has had to carefully manage the integration of the three cellar children with their "upstairs" siblings—Lisa, 16, Monika, 14, and Alexander, 12—who had grown up believing their mother had abandoned them to join a religious cult.

Therapists say the siblings have formed a tight, protective bond. The teenagers spend their days taking school lessons tailored to their unique circumstances, playing sports inside the clinic's courtyard, and watching movies together. 

"They are a remarkably resilient family," said Christoph Herbst, the attorney representing Elisabeth and the children. "They have shown incredible strength. The children play together, they laugh, and Elisabeth is an exceptionally devoted mother who lives entirely for her children's well-being."

Herbst noted that Elisabeth, despite losing her entire young adulthood, displays extraordinary mental fortitude. She is reportedly receiving intensive trauma counseling but is focused primarily on shielding her children from the media spotlight.

### Looking to the Future

While the family heals, the legal process against the man who inflicted their suffering moves forward. Josef Fritzl, 73, remains in a high-security prison in Sankt Pölten, awaiting trial on charges of rape, incest, false imprisonment, and murder by negligence related to the infant who died in the cellar. His trial is expected to begin early next year.

Elisabeth has already provided extensive videotaped testimony to prosecutors, ensuring she will not have to face her father in court.

For the doctors and staff at the Mauer clinic, the ultimate goal is to prepare the family for life outside the institution. Plans are already underway to relocate Elisabeth and her children to a secret location in Austria, where they will be provided with new identities and a custom-built home equipped with top-tier security.

For now, the family remains inside their protected sanctuary, taking life one day at a time under the sunlight they were denied for so long. 

"They have survived the unimaginable," Dr. Kepplinger said. "Now, they are finally getting the chance to live."

**SHADOWS OF THE CELLAR: The Deep Psychological Scars of Long-Term Captivity**

**VIENNA —** When Elisabeth Fritzl stepped out of a windowless subterranean bunker in Amstetten, Austria, in April 2008, she ended a 24-year physical ordeal at the hands of her father, Josef Fritzl. Yet for clinical psychologists and trauma experts worldwide, her liberation marked only the beginning of a complex, lifelong psychological recovery process. 

The Fritzl case—in which Elisabeth was held captive from age 18 to 42 and bore seven children in a cramped, soundproof basement—remains one of the most extreme examples of long-term forced confinement in modern history. The case has provided medical professionals with profound, albeit harrowing, insights into the limits of human psychological resilience.

### The Anatomy of Subterranean Trauma

The psychological toll of long-term captivity is multifaceted, involving acute Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), severe agoraphobia, disrupted cognitive development, and profound identity dissociation. 

According to medical experts who studied the case, captive environments characterized by sensory deprivation and absolute control create a distinct psychological landscape often referred to informally as "dungeon syndrome." 

"When a human being is deprived of natural light, spatial variety, and basic autonomy for decades, the brain fundamentally rewires itself to survive," explains Dr. Thomas Müller, a European clinical psychologist specializing in severe trauma. "The biological clock is shattered, emotional regulation collapses, and the concept of trust is entirely erased. For victims like Elisabeth and her children who were born underground, the outside world is not initially perceived as safe—it is perceived as an overwhelming, terrifying sensory assault."

Experts note that for the children who spent their entire lives in the cellar, the psychological hurdles were compounded by developmental deficits. Lacking normal social interactions, physical space to run, or exposure to sunlight, their spatial awareness and emotional processing were severely altered.

"The human mind adapts to a microscopic world," Dr. Müller added. "Moving from a low-ceilinged room into an open sky can induce panic attacks akin to severe vertigo. The brain simply does not know how to process infinite space after decades of confinement."

### Insight from Natascha Kampusch

The Fritzl revelations sent shockwaves through Austria, echoing the case of Natascha Kampusch, who was kidnapped in 1998 at age 10 and held in a secret cellar by Wolfgang Priklopil for eight years before her escape in 2006. 

Kampusch, who has since become an author and advocate, spoke publicly about the profound psychological burden shared by victims of subterranean prolonged captivity following the discovery of the Fritzl family.

"I can empathize deeply with what Elisabeth and her children are going through," Kampusch stated in an interview following the exposure of the Fritzl case. "The hardest part of coming out is not just facing the light, but facing the reality of lost time. You have to rebuild a personality that was systematically broken down every single day."

Kampusch detailed the survival mechanisms required to endure years of solitary or controlled confinement, emphasizing that victims often develop a split psychological reality to endure abuse.

"To survive, you construct an inner sanctuary," Kampusch explained. "You have to detach your mind from what is happening to your body. But when you are free, uniting those two halves of yourself takes years of immense effort and pain. The media and the public often expect a quick return to 'normalcy,' but there is no normal to return to—you have to create a completely new existence."

### Trauma Bonding and the Myth of Compliance

A central focus for psychological research stemming from the Fritzl case is the mechanism of survival compliance. Often mischaracterized by the public as "Stockholm Syndrome," trauma experts emphasize that subservience to an abuser in long-term captivity is a calculated, often unconscious survival strategy rather than genuine affection.

"In an environment of absolute control, where the perpetrator controls access to food, light, and life itself, total compliance is the only rational choice," says Dr. Max Friedrich, the child psychiatrist who led the medical team caring for Natascha Kampusch after her escape. "The victim must learn to read the abuser’s mood micro-expressions to stay alive. Unlearning that hyper-vigilance takes decades of intensive therapy."

Dr. Friedrich emphasized that recovery requires creating a completely safe environment where the victim retains 100 percent of the control they were previously denied.

### The Road to Rehabilitation

In the years following their release, Elisabeth Fritzl and her children were integrated into a specialized medical facility in Austria before being relocated to a private, undisclosed location under new identities. Reports from Austrian health authorities indicated that recovery involved intensive speech therapy, occupational therapy, and gradual exposure to the outside world.

While physical health can often be restored through proper diet, medical care, and sunlight, trauma experts agree that the psychological scars of cases like Fritzl's never fully disappear. 

"Freedom is not a cure-all; it is merely the arena in which healing can begin," says Dr. Müller. "Victims of long-term captivity do not simply 'move on.' With proper psychological support, privacy, and time, they learn to carry the weight of their past while slowly building a future."

The sudden availability of open space has also required physical adjustment. Having grown up in rooms barely two meters (six feet) high, the children initially struggled with spatial awareness, walking with stooped postures and exhibiting anxiety when introduced to large, open rooms.

"They have to learn how to move in a normal environment," Kepplinger explained, noting that the children lacked normal muscle development due to limited physical activity in the cellar.

#### Reuniting a fractured family

Inside the secluded clinic, medical personnel are working to help two distinct branches of the family form a single unit. Three of the children—Lisa, Monika, and Alexander—were taken upstairs by Josef Fritzl shortly after birth and raised by Fritzl and his wife, Rosemarie, as "foundlings." The other three surviving children remained trapped in the basement with Elisabeth. 

(A seventh child, a twin born in the cellar, died shortly after birth in 1996 and was cremated by Fritzl in a heating furnace, according to police reports.)

Doctors described the initial meeting between the "upstairs" and "downstairs" siblings as surprisingly warm, though emotionally intense. 

"The children are playing together, and the family is showing remarkable resilience," Kepplinger said. "Elisabeth is demonstrating extraordinary strength in guiding her children through this process."

The eldest daughter, 19-year-old Kerstin, remains in a medically induced coma at a local hospital suffering from severe organ failure—the emergency that initially led to the exposure of Fritzl’s crimes when Elisabeth pleaded to have her taken to a hospital.

#### A shielded environment

The clinic has taken extraordinary measures to shield the family from the intense global media interest surrounding the case. A dedicated suite has been set up with controlled lighting, soft furnishings, and high-level security to prevent photographers from invading their privacy.

Staff working with the family have been given specialized psychological support, and contact with the outside world remains strictly monitored to avoid overwhelming the survivors.

Psychiatrists caution that the rehabilitation process will take years, if not decades.

"We are dealing with a situation that has no precedent in modern medical history," Kepplinger stated. "Our priority is to provide them with safety, peace, and the time they need to build a life in the light."

Meanwhile, Josef Fritzl remains in custody in St. Pölten, facing charges including rape, incest, false imprisonment, and potentially murder by negligence relating to the infant who died in the cellar.

***

**Beyond the Cellar: Inside the Quiet Recovery of the Fritzl Family and the Legacy of Austria’s Darkest Crime**

**By** Tim Lister and Frederik Pleitgen, CNN  
**Updated** 8:00 AM EDT, Thursday, May 16, 2024

**(CNN) —** In a secluded, quiet village in countryside Austria—its exact location guarded like a state secret—a family lives under constant, watchful protection. The house features state-of-the-art security systems, thick perimeter hedges, and CCTV cameras designed to keep the outside world at bay. 

To passersby, they are just another local family attempting to lead a normal existence. But behind the closed doors lives Elisabeth Fritzl and her children, survivors of one of the most horrific crimes in modern European history.

More than fifteen years after the discovery of the subterranean dungeon where Elisabeth was imprisoned for 24 years by her own father, Josef Fritzl, the aftermath of the ordeal continues to ripple through Austria’s legal system, social conscience, and the lives of those who endured it.

---

[IMAGE PLACEHOLDER: A view of the house in Amstetten, Austria, where Elisabeth Fritzl was held captive for 24 years, pictured in 2008 before the cellar was filled with concrete. | Photo Credit: AP/File]

---

### A Fortress of Solitude and Healing

When police freed 42-year-old Elisabeth and six of her surviving children in April 2008, medical professionals warned that the psychological damage might be irreversible. Elisabeth had been lured into a windowless, soundproofed cellar beneath her family home in Amstetten in 1984, aged 18. Over the next two decades, she suffered continuous physical and sexual abuse at the hands of her father, giving birth to seven children in captivity. One infant died shortly after birth due to medical neglect and was cremated by Fritzl in an incinerator.

Three of the children lived in the cellar with Elisabeth, never seeing daylight until their rescue. The other three were taken upstairs by Fritzl and raised alongside his wife, Rosemarie, under the fabricated story that Elisabeth had abandoned them to join a cult.

In the immediate aftermath of their rescue, the entire family was housed at the Landesnervenklinik Mauer psychiatric hospital near Amstetten. Doctors worked painstakingly to reintroduce the subterranean family members to natural light, spatial awareness, and standard social interactions.

Today, Elisabeth—now in her late 50s—lives with her children in a custom-built home often referred to in Austrian media as "Village X." Reports from local authorities suggest she has successfully rebuilt a quiet, highly guarded life.

"They have shown extraordinary resilience," said Dr. Thomas Mueller, a forensic psychologist who followed the case closely during the trial. "The primary goal from day one was to prevent them from becoming permanent museum exhibits of tragedy. Through strict privacy laws and community protection, they were given the space to heal."

According to Austrian media reports, the family spent years in intensive therapy. The children who grew up upstairs and those raised in the cellar had to undergo a delicate process of bonding, having been kept entirely separate for decades despite living under the same roof. 

---

[IMAGE PLACEHOLDER: Police officers and forensic team members outside the Amstetten property shortly after the discovery of the subterranean bunker in April 2008. | Photo Credit: Getty Images]

---

### The Fate of Josef Fritzl

While Elisabeth and her family sought anonymity, Josef Fritzl became a symbol of incomprehensible evil. In March 2009, Fritzl pleaded guilty to all charges, including murder by negligence, rape, incest, false imprisonment, and enslavement. He was sentenced to life in a specialized institution for mentally disturbed offenders at Stein Prison in Krems an der Donau.

Now 89 years old, Fritzl’s physical and mental health has reportedly declined significantly. Austrian legal authorities confirmed earlier this year that Fritzl suffers from advanced dementia. 

In early 2024, a regional court in Krems considered a request by Fritzl’s legal team to transfer him from the high-security psychiatric unit to a standard prison facility—a move that could theoretically pave the way for conditional release to a nursing home due to his infirmity. 

"He is no longer a danger to society," Fritzl's attorney, Astrid Wagner, told reporters outside the courthouse earlier this year, citing his reduced mobility and cognitive decline. 

However, public opinion and legal experts remain fiercely opposed to any measures that could see Fritzl set free. For many in Austria, the thought of Fritzl spending his final days anywhere other than behind prison walls remains unbearable.

---

[IMAGE PLACEHOLDER: Courtroom sketch showing Josef Fritzl covering his face with a blue binder during his trial in Sankt Pölten, Austria, in March 2009. | Photo Credit: Reuters/File]

---

### Erasing the Footprints of Evil

For the town of Amstetten, a quiet industrial hub of 23,000 residents located 80 miles west of Vienna, the aftermath of the case was an ordeal of its own. For months after the discovery, the town was besieged by international media, tourists seeking ghoulish thrills, and satellite trucks.

Local authorities took drastic measures to ensure the site of the horror could not become a permanent monument to Fritzl's crimes. 

In 2013, the house on Ybbsstrasse was completely gutted. The subterranean bunker—a labyrinth of reinforced concrete doors, electronic keypads, and low ceilings—was completely filled with 300 cubic meters of liquid concrete. The property was later sold to a private buyer, redesigned, and converted into apartments, with strict provisions prohibiting any commercialization of its history.

"It was vital for the town to heal," said a former local government official who asked not to be named. "We could not allow Amstetten to be defined solely by the monster who lived among us."

### Institutional Reform and Systemic Lessons

The Fritzl case, alongside the earlier abduction of Natascha Kampusch—who was held captive in a cellar near Vienna for eight years before escaping in 2006—forced Austria to confront uncomfortable questions about its social welfare systems, police oversight, and community vigilance.

Critics questioned how Fritzl was able to build an elaborate underground bunker, install heavy blast doors, and move massive amounts of building materials without raising suspicion from municipal inspectors or neighbors. Questions were also raised regarding how social services allowed Fritzl to adopt three of Elisabeth's children without verifying her whereabouts.

In the years following the trial, Austria instituted reforms to its social welfare reporting mechanisms and increased background checks for foster care and adoption procedures. Legal definitions surrounding sexual violence and false imprisonment were also toughened within the Austrian criminal code.

### A Legacy of Survival

Despite the shadow cast by Josef Fritzl's actions, the enduring story of the case has shifted over the past decade from one of unimaginable horror to one of remarkable human survival.

Elisabeth Fritzl has never granted an interview to the press, fiercely guarding her privacy and that of her children. Offers totaling millions of dollars from international media outlets have been consistently rejected. 

Those who have assisted the family over the years say this silence has been key to their survival.

"The ultimate victory over Josef Fritzl was not just the life sentence he received in court," said Dr. Mueller. "The ultimate victory is that Elisabeth and her children were able to reclaim their lives, their dignity, and their freedom—far away from the darkness he built for them."
